newsitem.title: UK: BA still hit by staff shortage after strike.
newsitem.headline: BA still hit by staff shortage after strike.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Wednesday that flights out of London Heathrow were unlikely to be back to normal until Monday because of staff shortages following last week's cabin crew strike.

Services out of London Gatwick are already back to normal. But the airline said it planned to operate only about 60 percent of its short-haul flights and 85 percent of long-haul services out of Heathrow on Wednesday, because so many cabin staff who went on sick leave during the strike had still not returned to work.
BA expected to operate only around 60 percent of Heathrow short-haul services on Friday and 90 to 95 percent of long haul flights.

A company spokesman said staff gradually had been returning to work since the strike ended last Friday but over 1,300 cabin staff were still off sick this morning, about twice the normal rate at this time of the year.
Nearly 2,000 cabin crew registered for sick leave last week, which BA said left only 313 staff deemed actually to be on strike.

The airline and the BASSA cabin crew union have agreed to reopen talks in the dispute over pay, after BASSA offered to make new proposals on how to find the 42 million pounds of savings sought by management from a new pay structure.
BA urged BASSA on Wednesday to make the proposals as soon as possible so that talks could begin.
"It's of the greatest urgency," said a spokesman. "There's still uncertainty for our customers and we want to settle this dispute as soon as possible."
BASSA's parent union the Transport and General Workers' Union (T&G) said that BA should get the proposals later today.
"We're sending our proposals over to BA today and then we hope for talks to start later in the week," said T&G spokesman Andrew Murray.
But the uncertainty for travellers was set to last some time yet. Murray said negotiations were expected to take two to three weeks.

BA chief executive Robert Ayling said yesterday that the strike had already cost the company "tens of millions of pounds" as well as lost bookings for the future and urged BASSA to adopt a "constructive approach."
The 3,000 members of the breakaway union, Cabin Crew 89 which represents about 25 percent of BA's cabin staff, have already accepted the company's new pay package.
